title: Saying who you are
intro: Turkish has no separate verb for **am**, **are** and **is**. Instead, a short ending on the noun or adjective does the job: *öğrenci* (student), *öğrenciyim* (I am a student). This unit adds the second kind of vowel harmony, the personal pronouns, the endings of **to be**, and the buffer letter that joins two vowels. It also introduces the notation used in grammars of Turkish from now on.

blocks.text: In [unit 2](a1-u02) you met two-way harmony: a suffix with *e* or *a*. Many other suffixes have a high vowel instead, and it comes in four forms: *ı*, *i*, *u* or *ü*. Again the last vowel of the word decides, but now both questions from the [vowel chart](gp-vowel-groups) count: front or back, and rounded or not.

Put simply, the suffix vowel copies the last vowel's position and rounding. After a back unrounded vowel you get *ı*, after a front unrounded vowel *i*, after a back rounded vowel *u*, after a front rounded vowel *ü*. Your mouth hardly moves between the two syllables.

blocks.text: From now on, this course writes suffixes in the short notation most grammars of Turkish use. A capital letter stands for a vowel or consonant that changes with harmony, and letters in brackets appear only in some words.

blocks.text: Keep the two kinds apart. A two-way suffix never has *ı*, *i*, *u* or *ü* (*kitaplar*, never *kitaplır*), and a four-way suffix never has *a* or *e* (*açım*, never *açam*).

sections.title: I, you, he, she: the personal pronouns

head: Pronoun
Meaning
rows: you (several people, or one person politely)

blocks.text: *O* covers he, she and it: Turkish has no grammatical gender. It is the same word as *o* (that over there) from [unit 2](gp-demonstratives), and *onlar* (they) is the same as *onlar* (those).

Because the ending already shows the person, the pronoun is usually dropped: *Öğretmenim* is enough for I am a teacher. Use the pronoun to contrast or stress: *Ben öğretmenim, sen öğrencisin* (I'm the teacher, you're the student).

*Sen* is for family, friends, children and people your own age in relaxed settings. *Siz* is for more than one person, and for one person you address politely: a stranger, a shopkeeper, an older person, your manager. When in doubt, use *siz*; people will tell you if they'd rather you used *sen*.

items.en: I'm the teacher, you're the student.

blocks.text: *Sen* and *siz* work like French “tu” and “vous”: *siz* is both the plural and the polite form.
In the present, **to be** is a set of endings added to a noun or an adjective. Grammars call them the type I personal endings; you'll meet a second set, for the past tense, in A2.

rows.en: he or she is a teacher
you are a teacher (polite), you are teachers
he or she is a doctor
you are a doctor (polite), you are doctors

blocks.title: *hasta* (ill): a word ending in a vowel

blocks.text: **The third person** has no ending: *O öğretmen* (she is a teacher), *Ali yorgun* (Ali is tired). In writing, on signs, in definitions and in formal statements you'll often see `-DIr` instead: *Ali öğretmendir.* In conversation it can sound like **surely** or **must be**, a use you'll study in C1, so for now use the bare form when you speak. After a voiceless consonant the *d* becomes *t*: *Türk'tür*, *kitaptır*; more on that in [unit 5](gp-consonant-assimilation).
**They** takes `-lAr`, but when *onlar* is already in the sentence the ending is often left out: *Onlar öğretmen* and *Onlar öğretmenler* both mean they are teachers.
**Stress.** The endings of **to be** are never stressed. The stress stays on the word they follow: *öğretMENim*, *dokTORsun*, *hasTAyım*.

blocks.title: Apostrophes on nationalities
blocks.text: Names of nations are proper nouns, so the ending follows an apostrophe: *Türk'üm*, *Fransız'ım*, *Alman'sınız*. Words built with `-lI` (from), such as *Kanadalı* and *İstanbullu*, are new words and take no apostrophe: *Kanadalıyım*. The apostrophe rule is covered in full in [unit 5](gp-apostrophe).
The negative (*öğretmen değilim*, I am not a teacher) and the question (*öğretmen misin?*, are you a teacher?) come in [unit 4](a1-u04).

sections.title: Buffer letters: the y in öğrenciyim

blocks.text: Turkish avoids two vowels side by side where a suffix joins a word. When a word ends in a vowel and the suffix starts with one, a buffer letter (*kaynaştırma harfi*) slips in between. For the endings of **to be**, the buffer is *y*: *öğrenci* + `-Im` → *öğrenciyim*.

Only the endings that start with a vowel need it, so the endings for *sen* and *siz* never do: *öğrencisin*, *hastasınız*. After a consonant there is no buffer: *öğretmenim*, *doktoruz*. That is what the brackets in `-(y)Im` and `-(y)Iz` mean.
You already know one of these forms: *iyiyim* from [unit 1](a1-u01) is *iyi* + *y* + *-im*.
Other suffixes use other buffers: *s* in *arabası* (his car, [unit 9](gp-possessive-suffixes)) and *n* in *arabanın* (of the car, [unit 10](gp-genitive)). You'll meet them one at a time.
The *y* belongs to neither the word nor the ending. Don't add it after a consonant: *öğretmenim*, never *öğretmenyim*.

summary: Four-way harmony: after *a, ı* → *ı*; after *e, i* → *i*; after *o, u* → *u*; after *ö, ü* → *ü*.
Notation: `A` = e/a, `I` = ı/i/u/ü; a letter in brackets, as in `-(y)Im`, appears only after a vowel.
Pronouns: *ben, sen, o, biz, siz, onlar*. *O* is he, she and it; *siz* is plural or polite. Pronouns are usually dropped.
To be is an ending: `-(y)Im`, `-sIn`, `-∅`, `-(y)Iz`, `-sInIz`, `-lAr`: *öğretmenim, öğretmensin, öğretmen…*
`-DIr` is a formal or written third person: *Ali öğretmendir*. In speech, use the bare form.
Nation names take an apostrophe before the ending (*Türk'üm*); words in `-lI` do not (*Kanadalıyım*).
